package.title: Tirzepatide Not Working Yet? What the 72-Week Trial Shows

social.instagram_caption:
Tirzepatide not working yet? If you're a few weeks in and wondering, here's the trial context.

Here's what the trial actually shows:
→ In SURMOUNT-1, doses started low and were raised every 4 weeks
→ The 15 mg group didn't reach full dose until week 20 of 72
→ The main result — tirzepatide 15 mg (n=630) averaging −20.9% vs placebo (n=643) at −3.1% — was measured at week 72, not week 4
→ That's an average % of body weight across the group. Individual results varied, and this was studied in adults with BMI 30+ (or 27+ with a weight-related condition), without diabetes

Save this for your next check-in, and bring your own progress questions to your prescriber.

Common side effects in the trial were mostly mild to moderate and showed up most during dose increases — think nausea, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting.

sources.title: Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity (SURMOUNT-1; online June 4, 2022; print July 21, 2022; N Engl J Med 387:205-216)

factcheck.summary: The SURMOUNT-1 facts on the slides check out against the trial and secondary summaries of it. The trial had 2,539 adults with BMI 30 or higher, or BMI 27 or higher with at least one weight-related condition, and people with diabetes were excluded. Participants were split 1:1:1:1 between 5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg and placebo, all with lifestyle advice. Every tirzepatide group started at 2.5 mg and went up by 2.5 mg every 4 weeks, so the 15 mg group reached its full dose at week 20. At week 72 the average weight change was −20.9% on 15 mg versus −3.1% on placebo, using the treatment-regimen estimand. Side effects were mainly digestive, mostly mild to moderate, and happened mostly while doses were going up. The group sizes (630/636/630/643) match the published paper as I know it, but I couldn't reopen the paper in this session to re-check them. The citation details are correct: NEJM 387:205-216, online June 4, 2022, print July 21, 2022. The safety lines are there: "don't stop or change your medicines on your own", "your prescriber decides your dose", the disclaimer and the prescriber line. There is no dosing advice. The only problems are three small framing points with exact fixes below. Note on the source: the NEJM URL is the correct page for the article but returned 403 to the automated fetcher. That is bot-blocking, not a dead link, and it opens normally in a browser.

issues.claim: In SURMOUNT-1, the main result was measured after 72 weeks, not in the first few weeks.
issues.problem: This is true, but next to a 'not working yet?' hook a reader could take it to mean that losing no weight for months is normal. In the trial, average weight loss started early and kept going during the dose increases. The slides only show the week-72 endpoint, so the wording should not suggest a delay.
issues.fix: Replace the slide 7 body with: "In SURMOUNT-1, the main result was measured at week 72, after doses were raised over the first 20 weeks. If you're unsure about your progress, ask your prescriber. Not personal advice: talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you."

issues.claim: Common side effects and what to do
issues.problem: The headline promises 'what to do' about side effects, but the slide only lists the side effects, says not to change medicines alone, and suggests taking notes. It gives no tips for making them easier, so the title promises more than the slide delivers.
issues.fix: Change the headline to: "Common side effects and when to speak up"

issues.problem: This is the myth, written as a plain statement. If the template doesn't clearly label it as a MYTH, someone scrolling past could read it as the channel's own claim.
issues.fix: Change the headline to: "Myth: trial averages predict my results"
